### Polynomial regression and step functions (ISLRv2 Applied 6) {#sec-exr-wage-poly}

<!-- No slidebreak between this
heading and the div that follows. The preceding slidebreak already opens a fresh
slide; the heading and this div intentionally share that slide to avoid a
title-only slide. -->
::::{#exr-wage-polynomial-cv}

Using the `Wage` dataset from the `ISLR2` package [@james2021islr2e]:

**(a)** Use 10-fold cross-validation to choose the polynomial degree $d^*$ for predicting `wage` from `age`.
Plot the CV errors for degrees 1 through 10.

**(b)** Fit the degree-$d^*$ polynomial and plot it with a 95% confidence band.

**(c)** Separately, choose the number of cut-points $K^*$ for a step-function model using cross-validation.
Plot the chosen step-function fit.

::::


{{< slidebreak >}}

::::{#sol-wage-polynomial-cv}

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### R

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(ISLR2)
library(boot)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1)
cv_poly <- vapply(1:10, function(d) {
  cv.glm(Wage, glm(wage ~ poly(age, d), data = Wage), K = 10)$delta[1]
}, numeric(1))
best_d <- which.min(cv_poly)
cat("CV-selected degree:", best_d, "\n")
plot(1:10, cv_poly, type = "b", xlab = "Degree", ylab = "CV MSE",
     main = "Polynomial degree selection")
points(best_d, cv_poly[best_d], col = "red", pch = 19)
```

**(b)** Fit the degree-$d^*$ [polynomial](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-polynomial) and draw its 95% confidence band:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
age_grid <- data.frame(age = seq(min(Wage$age), max(Wage$age)))
fit_best <- lm(wage ~ poly(age, best_d), data = Wage)
band <- cbind(age_grid,
              predict(fit_best, age_grid, interval = "confidence"))
ggplot(Wage, aes(age, wage)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(y = fit, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr),
              alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = band, aes(y = fit), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Wage")
```

**(c)** Choose the number of cut-points $K^*$ for the step function.
A step function with $K$ cut-points has $K + 1$ intervals, so `cut(age, K + 1)` makes it:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
cv_step <- vapply(1:9, function(K) {
  wage_cut <- transform(Wage, age_cut = cut(age, K + 1))
  cv.glm(wage_cut, glm(wage ~ age_cut, data = wage_cut), K = 10)$delta[1]
}, numeric(1))
best_K <- which.min(cv_step)
cat("CV-selected number of cut-points:", best_K, "\n")

fit_step <- lm(wage ~ cut(age, best_K + 1), data = Wage)
step_df <- cbind(age_grid, fit = predict(fit_step, age_grid))
ggplot(Wage, aes(age, wage)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = step_df, aes(y = fit), colour = "tomato", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Wage")
```

#### Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| python.reticulate: false
# Not run: the rme render has no Python environment.
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score
from ISLP import load_data
Wage = load_data("Wage")
X = Wage["age"].values.reshape(-1, 1)
y = Wage["wage"].values
folds = KFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=1)

# Standardize age first: raw age**10 is of order 1e17, which makes the
# least-squares problem ill-conditioned (the R solution uses orthogonal poly()).
cv_errs = [-cross_val_score(
    Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()),
              ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(d, include_bias=False)),
              ("reg", LinearRegression())]),
    X, y, cv=folds, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").mean()
    for d in range(1, 11)]
best_d = int(np.argmin(cv_errs)) + 1
print(f"CV-selected degree: {best_d}")

# (b) Degree-best_d fit with a 95% confidence band
age_lo, age_hi = Wage["age"].min(), Wage["age"].max()
age_grid = np.linspace(age_lo, age_hi, age_hi - age_lo + 1)
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X)
poly = PolynomialFeatures(best_d)
fit_poly = sm.OLS(y, poly.fit_transform(scaler.transform(X))).fit()
pred = fit_poly.get_prediction(
    poly.transform(scaler.transform(age_grid.reshape(-1, 1)))
).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)
plt.scatter(Wage["age"], Wage["wage"], alpha=0.15, s=6)
plt.plot(age_grid, pred["mean"], color="steelblue", linewidth=2)
plt.fill_between(age_grid, pred["mean_ci_lower"], pred["mean_ci_upper"],
                 alpha=0.3)
plt.xlabel("Age"); plt.ylabel("Wage"); plt.show()

# (c) Step function: K cut-points make K + 1 intervals
def step_cv(K):
    cut = pd.cut(Wage["age"], K + 1)
    dummies = pd.get_dummies(cut, drop_first=True).astype(float).values
    return -cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), dummies, y, cv=folds,
                            scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").mean()
step_errs = [step_cv(K) for K in range(1, 10)]
best_K = int(np.argmin(step_errs)) + 1
print(f"CV-selected number of cut-points: {best_K}")

cut, bins = pd.cut(Wage["age"], best_K + 1, retbins=True)
fit_step = LinearRegression().fit(
    pd.get_dummies(cut, drop_first=True).astype(float).values, y)
grid_cut = pd.cut(age_grid, bins, include_lowest=True)
step_pred = fit_step.predict(
    pd.get_dummies(grid_cut, drop_first=True).astype(float).values)
plt.scatter(Wage["age"], Wage["wage"], alpha=0.15, s=6)
plt.plot(age_grid, step_pred, color="tomato", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Age"); plt.ylabel("Wage"); plt.show()
```

:::

### Backfitting algorithm (ESL §9.1.1 / ISLRv2 Applied 11) {#sec-exr-backfitting}

<!-- No slidebreak between this
heading and the div that follows. The preceding slidebreak already opens a fresh
slide; the heading and this div intentionally share that slide to avoid a
title-only slide. -->
::::{#exr-backfitting}

The **backfitting algorithm** [@hastie2009esl2e, §9.1.1] fits an additive model
$Y = \a + \sum_j f_j(X_j) + \eps$ by iteratively smoothing partial residuals.

For $p=2$ predictors with linear component smoothers $\est{f_j}(X_j) = \eb_j X_j$:

1. Initialise: $\est{\a} = \bar{y}$, $\est{f_1} = \est{f_2} = 0$.
2. Repeat until convergence (Gauss--Seidel order --- re-centre each
   $\est{f_j}$ immediately, so the centred $\est{f_1}$ is used when
   computing $r_2$):
   a. $r_1 \leftarrow y - \est{\a} - \est{f_2}(x_2)$; regress $r_1$ on
      $x_1$ to update $\est{f_1}$; $\est{f_1} \leftarrow \est{f_1} -
      \overline{\est{f_1}}$.
   b. $r_2 \leftarrow y - \est{\a} - \est{f_1}(x_1)$; regress $r_2$ on
      $x_2$ to update $\est{f_2}$; $\est{f_2} \leftarrow \est{f_2} -
      \overline{\est{f_2}}$.

**(a)** Implement this on simulated data with known true coefficients.

**(b)** Verify the coefficients match `lm(y ~ x1 + x2)`.

::::


{{< slidebreak >}}

::::{#sol-backfitting}

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### R

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
set.seed(1)
n <- 100
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rnorm(n)
y <- 2 + 3 * x1 - 1.5 * x2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
alpha_hat <- mean(y)
f1 <- f2 <- rep(0, n)
for (iter in seq_len(500)) {
  r1 <- y - alpha_hat - f2
  b1 <- coef(lm(r1 ~ x1))[2]
  f1 <- b1 * x1
  f1 <- f1 - mean(f1)
  r2 <- y - alpha_hat - f1
  b2 <- coef(lm(r2 ~ x2))[2]
  f2 <- b2 * x2
  f2 <- f2 - mean(f2)
}
lm_fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2)
cat(sprintf("Backfitting: b1=%.4f, b2=%.4f\n", b1, b2))
cat(sprintf("lm():        b1=%.4f, b2=%.4f\n",
            coef(lm_fit)[2], coef(lm_fit)[3]))
```

#### Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| python.reticulate: false
# Not run: the rme render has no Python environment.
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 100; x1 = rng.standard_normal(n); x2 = rng.standard_normal(n)
y = 2 + 3*x1 - 1.5*x2 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
alpha_hat = y.mean(); f1 = np.zeros(n); f2 = np.zeros(n)
for _ in range(500):
    r1 = y - alpha_hat - f2
    b1 = float(np.cov(x1, r1)[0, 1] / np.var(x1, ddof=1))
    f1 = b1*x1 - (b1*x1).mean()
    r2 = y - alpha_hat - f1
    b2 = float(np.cov(x2, r2)[0, 1] / np.var(x2, ddof=1))
    f2 = b2*x2 - (b2*x2).mean()
X_ols = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x1, x2])
b_ols = np.linalg.lstsq(X_ols, y, rcond=None)[0]
print(f"Backfitting: b1={b1:.4f}, b2={b2:.4f}")
print(f"OLS:         b1={b_ols[1]:.4f}, b2={b_ols[2]:.4f}")
```

:::

The coefficients agree, confirming backfitting converges to OLS when
all component smoothers are linear [@hastie2009esl2e, §9.1.1].
